Includes the open problem of widening and the privacy monitor use.

atoms.statement: In Rely, the reliability of an integer expression e is the probability that it evaluates to the same value n in an unreliable evaluation as in the fully reliable evaluation.

evidence.text: To illustrate the intuition behind this design point, consider the evaluation of an integer expression e.
The reliability of e is the probability that it evaluates to the same value n in an unreliable evaluation as in the fully reliable evaluation.

atoms.statement: The joint reliability of a set of parameters is the probability that they all have the correct value when passed in from the caller, and it is a key abstraction for Rely's verification.

evidence.text: The joint reliability of a set of parameters is the probability that they all have the correct value when passed in from the caller.
The joint reliability is a key abstraction for our verification; we will formalize it in Section 15.4.2.

atoms.statement: A Rely reliability specification expresses the reliability of a function's results, when executed on an unreliable hardware platform, as a function of the reliabilities of its inputs; for example, int<0.99*R(pblocks,cblock)> states that the return value is an integer whose reliability is at least 99% of the joint reliability of pblocks and cblock.

evidence.text: Rely’s reliability specifications express the reliability of a function’s results – when executed on an unreliable hardware platform – as a function of the reliabil-
ities of its inputs. The specification for the reliability of search_ref’s result is int<0.99*R(pblocks,cblock)>.
This states that the return value is an integer with a reliability that is at least 99% of the joint reliability of the parameters pblocks and cblock (denoted by R(pblocks, cblock)).

atoms.statement: For an assignment $x = e$, the precondition generator substitutes into each joint reliability factor $\mathcal{R}(\{x\}\cup X)$ a new factor $\rho_1(e)\cdot\psi(wr(\Lambda(x)))\cdot\mathcal{R}(\rho_2(e)\cup X)$, where $\rho_1(e)\cdot\psi(wr(\Lambda(x)))$ is the probability that e evaluates fully reliably and its value is reliably written to the memory location of x.

evidence.text: The substitution Q[(ρ1(e) · ψ(wr(Λ(x))) · R(ρ2(e)∪X))/R({x}∪X)] binds each reliability factor in which x occurs – R({x}∪X) – and replaces the factor with a new reliability factor R(ρ2(e) ∪X) where ρ2(e) is the set of variables referenced by e.
The substitution also multiplies the reliability factor by ρ1(e)·ψ(wr(Λ(x))), which is the probability that e evaluates fully reliably and its value is reliably written to the memory location for x.

atoms.statement: Rely's reliability analysis works backward from a postcondition requiring each array argument's reliability to meet its specification, generating a reliability precondition (a conjunction of predicates $A_{out} \le r \cdot \mathcal{R}(X)$) such that if the precondition holds on function entry, the postcondition holds at function end, and a checker then decides whether the specifications satisfy it.

evidence.text: A reliability precondition is a conjunction of predicates of the form Aout ≤r · R(X), where Aout is a placeholder for a developer-provided reliability specification for an output with name out, r is a numerical value between 0 and 1, and the term R(X) is the joint
reliability of the set X of variables (including the function parameters) on entry to the function.

The analysis starts at the end of the function from a postcondition that must be true when the function returns and then works backward to produce a precondition such that if the precondition holds before execution of the function, then the postcondition holds at the end of the function.

atoms.statement: Rely's analysis starts from a postcondition at the end of a function and works backward to produce a precondition such that, if the precondition holds before execution of the function, then the postcondition holds at the end.

evidence.text: The analysis starts at the end of the function from a postcondition that must be true when the function returns and then works backward to produce a precondition such that if the precondition holds before execution of the function, then the postcondition holds at the end of the function.

atoms.statement: Rely's analysis conservatively approximates the reliability of a computation by considering only the scenario in which the unreliable evaluation encounters no faults, and ignores the scenario in which faults occur but the correct value is still returned by chance.

evidence.text: There are two ways that an unreliable evaluation can return n: (1) the unreliable evaluation of e encounters no faults and (2) the unreliable evaluation possibly encounters faults, but still returns n by chance.
Rely’s analysis conservatively approximates the reliability of a computation by only considering the first scenario.

atoms.statement: For an unbounded while loop, a variable that is modified unreliably within the loop and has a loop-carried dependence has reliability that decreases monotonically with the number of iterations, so the only sound approximation of its reliability is zero.

evidence.text: The reliability of a variable that is modified unreliably within a loop and has a loop-carried dependence is a monotonically decreasing function of the number of loop iterations.
The only sound approximation of the reliability of such a variable is therefore zero.

atoms.statement: Because Rely's analysis considers only the probability that a result is computed fully reliably, it requires only a hardware reliability specification giving the probability that each arithmetic/logical and memory operation executes correctly, is oblivious to the computation's input distribution, and does not require a full model of how soft errors affect its result.

evidence.text: As a consequence, the analysis requires as input only a hardware reliability specification that gives the probability with which each arithmetic/logical operation and memory operation executes correctly.
The analysis is therefore oblivious to a computation’s input distribution and does not require a full model of how soft errors affect its result.

atoms.statement: The RDF Mapping Language (RML) expresses customized mapping rules from heterogeneous data structures, formats and serializations to RDF.

evidence.text: The RDF Mapping Language (RML) [110,111] expresses customized mapping rules from heterogeneous data structures, formats and serializations to RDF.

atoms.statement: RML is a superset of R2RML that aims to extend R2RML's applicability and broaden its scope by adding support for heterogeneous data.

evidence.text: RML is a superset of R2RML, aiming to extend its applicability and broaden its scope, adding support for heterogeneous data.

atoms.statement: RML keeps the mapping rules as in R2RML but excludes R2RML's database-specific references from the core model, so input data limited to one database in R2RML becomes a broad set of one or more input data sources in RML.

evidence.text: RML keeps the mapping rules as in R2RML but excludes its database-specific references from the core model.

This way, the input data that is limited to a certain database in R2RML (because each R2RML processor may be associated to only one database), becomes a broad set of one or more input data sources in RML.

atoms.statement: RML's Reference Formulation declaration (rml:referenceFormulation) indicates the formulation, such as a standard, query language or grammar (e.g., XPath for XML or JSONPath for JSON), used to refer to the data, which lets the mapping definitions that generate RDF terms and triples stay generic.

evidence.text: Thus, a dedicated way of referring to the data’s fractions is considered, while the mapping definitions that define how the RDF terms and triples are generated remain generic.
RML considers that any reference to the Logical Source should be defined in a form relevant to the input data, e.g. XPath for XML data or JSONPath for JSON data.

To this end, the Reference Formulation (rml:referenceFormulation) declaration is introduced (Listing 4.7, line 4), indicating the formulation (for instance, a standard, query language or grammar) used to refer to its data.

atoms.statement: The Function Map (fnml:FunctionMap) is a Term Map introduced as an RML extension to align RML with FnO, generating its term as the output value of an executed function instead of from a constant or a reference to raw data values.

evidence.text: The Function Map (fnml:FunctionMap) is another Term Map, introduced as an extension of RML, to facilitate the alignment of the two, RML and FnO.
A Function Map is generated by executing a function instead of using a constant or a reference to the raw data values.
Once the function is executed, its output value is the term generated by this Function Map.

atoms.statement: RML's Logical Source extends R2RML's Logical Table by using rml:source to specify the source of the original data, whereas the R2RML Logical Table only determines a database table through rr:tableName.

evidence.text: Logical Source. RML’s Logical Source (rml:LogicalSource, Listing 4.5) extends R2RML’s Logical Table and determines the data source with the data to generate the knowledge graph.
In the case of RML, a broader reference to any input source is required.
Thus, the Logical Source (rml:source) is introduced to specify the source with the original data.

atoms.statement: In RML the iterator (rml:iterator) determines the iteration pattern over the data source and specifies the extract of the data taken during each iteration.

evidence.text: Thereafter, the iterator (rml:iterator) is introduced (Listing 4.7, line 5).
The iterator determines the iteration pattern over the data source and specifies the extract of the data during each iteration.

atoms.statement: RML's logical reference generalizes R2RML's column name reference, and its value must be a valid expression according to the Reference Formulation defined at the Logical Source.

evidence.text: In the case of RML, a more generic notion is introduced, the logical reference.
Its value must be a valid reference to the data of the input dataset according to the specified reference formulation.
Thus, the reference’s value should be a valid expression according to the Reference Formulation defined at the Logical Source.

atoms.statement: RML's Language Map (rml:LanguageMap) extends R2RML's rr:language by allowing not only constant language values but also references derived from the input data, with rr:language regarded as an abbreviation of rml:languageMap.

evidence.text: Language Map. RML introduces a new Term Map for defining the language, the Language Map (rml:LanguageMap, Listing 4.10, line 5), which extends R2RML’s language tag (rr:language).

The Language Map allows not only constant values for language but also references derived from the input data. rr:language is considered then an abbreviation for the rml:languageMap, as rr:predicate is for the rr:predicateMap.

atoms.statement: RML leaves out of scope how an input data source is retrieved, in the same way that R2RML leaves out of scope how the SQL connection is established.

evidence.text: RML considers an original data source, but the way this input is retrieved remains out of scope, in the same way it remains out of scope for R2RML how the SQL connection is established.

atoms.statement: RML remains backwards compatible with R2RML because relational databases form a specific case of the generic way RML defines mapping rules over different data structures.

evidence.text: RML provides a generic way of defining mapping rules referring to different data structures, combined with case-specific extensions, but remains backwards compatible with R2RML, as relational databases form such a specific case.

atoms.statement: Unlike RML, which allows other query languages to be introduced through reference formulations, xR2RML originally specified the data format explicitly via xrr:format and decided exactly which query language to use, and later optionally considered a reference formulation to converge with RML.

evidence.text: In contrast to RML that considers a formulation (rml:referenceFormulation) to refer to its input data, xR2RML originally specified explicitly the format of data retrieved from the database using the property xrr:format (Listing 4.15, line 2).
While RML allows for other kinds of query languages to be introduced, xR2RML decides exactly which query language to use.
In an effort to converge with RML, xR2RML considers optionally a reference formulation.

atoms.statement: Data integration is the process of providing uniform access to a set of distributed (decentralised), autonomous, and heterogeneous data sources.

evidence.text: Data integration is the process of providing uniform access to a set of distributed (or decentralised), autonomous, and heterogeneous data sources [114].

atoms.statement: A data integration system is formally defined as a triple $I = \langle G, S, M \rangle$, where $G$ is the global schema, $S$ is the source schema, and $M$ is the mapping between $G$ and $S$.

evidence.text: A data integration system, I, is defined as a triple <G, S, M>, where:
– G is the global schema, expressed in a language LG over an alphabet AG.

The alphabet AS includes a symbol for each element of the sources. – M is the mapping between G and S, constituted by a set of assertions of the forms: qS →qG, qG →qS; where qS and qG are two queries of the same arity, respectively over the source schema S, and over the global schema G.

atoms.statement: A data integration system provides a global (mediated) schema that gives a reconciled view of all data available in the different data sources.

evidence.text: Data integration systems provide a global schema (also known as mediated schema) to provide a reconciled view of all data available in different data sources.

atoms.statement: In a data integration system, the mapping $M$ consists of assertions of the forms $q_S \rightarrow q_G$ and $q_G \rightarrow q_S$, where $q_S$ and $q_G$ are queries of the same arity over the source schema $S$ and the global schema $G$ respectively, and each assertion specifies the connection between elements of the global and source schemas.

evidence.text: The alphabet AS includes a symbol for each element of the sources. – M is the mapping between G and S, constituted by a set of assertions of the forms: qS →qG, qG →qS; where qS and qG are two queries of the same arity, respectively over the source schema S, and over the global schema G.
An assertion specifies the connection between the elements of the global schema and those of the source schema.

atoms.statement: Under the Global-as-View (GAV) approach, concepts of the global schema are defined as views over the data sources, so a query over the global schema is reformulated by query unfolding, i.e., rewriting it into a query that refers only to the source schema.

evidence.text: Rules defined using the Global-as-View (GAV) approach define concepts in the global schema as a set of views over the data sources.
A query posed over the global schema, G, needs to be reformulated by rewriting the query with the views defined in, M.
Such rewriting is also known as query unfolding – the process of rewriting
the query defined over global schema to a query that only refers to the source schema.

atoms.statement: Under the Local-as-View (LAV) approach, data sources are described as views over the global schema, with the mapping rules in $M$ associating a query over the global schema $G$ to each element of the source schema $S$.

evidence.text: Mappings specified using the Local-as-View (LAV) approach describe the data sources as views over the global schema, contrary to the GAV approach that defines the global schema as views over the data sources.
Using the LAV approach, the mapping rules in M associates a query defined over the global schema, G, to each elements of source schema, S.

atoms.statement: In the GAV approach, adding or removing sources may require updating all the mappings in the global schema, which requires knowledge of all the sources, whereas in LAV adding and removing sources is easier because sources are described independently of each other.

evidence.text: However, adding and removing sources in the GAV approach may involve updating all the mappings in the global schema, which requires knowledge of all the sources.
Adding and removing sources in LAV is easier than GAV, as data sources are described independently of each other.

atoms.statement: Because LAV can express incomplete information (the mapping may not contain corresponding sources for all global-schema elements), query answering in LAV may involve querying incomplete information, which is computationally more expensive.

evidence.text: In addition, it allows for expressing incomplete information as the global schema represents a database whose tuples are unknown, i.e., the mapping M defined by LAV approach might not contain all the corresponding sources for all the elements in the global schema, G.
As a result, query answering in LAV may consist of querying incomplete information, which is computationally more expensive [114].

atoms.statement: GAV mappings specify directly how to compute tuples of the global schema relations from tuples in the sources, which makes them easier to use for query unfolding.

evidence.text: Conceptually, GAV mappings specify directly how to compute tuples of the global schema relations from tuples in the sources.
This characteristics of GAV mappings makes them easier for query unfolding strategy.

atoms.statement: A federated query processing system provides a unified access interface to a set of autonomous, distributed, and heterogeneous data sources.

evidence.text: A federated query processing system2, provides a unified access interface to a set of autonomous, distributed, and heterogeneous data sources.

atoms.statement: The role of a federated query engine is to transform a query expressed in terms of the global schema (the federated query) into an equivalent query expressed in the schemas of the data sources (the local query).

evidence.text: The role of a federated query engine is to transform a query expressed in terms of the global schema, i.e., the federated query, into an equivalent query expressed in the schema of the data sources, i.e., local query.

atoms.statement: The main objective of federated query processing is to transform a query posed on a federation of data sources into a query composed of the union of subqueries over individual data sources of the federation.

evidence.text: The main objective of federated query processing is to transform a query posed on a federation of data sources into a query composed of the union of subqueries over individual data sources of the federation.

atoms.statement: Federated query processing conceptually involves four main sub-problems: data source description, query decomposition and source selection, query planning and optimization, and query execution.

evidence.text: Conceptually, federated query processing involves four main sub-problems (components): (i) data source description, (ii) query decomposition and source selection, (iii) query planning and optimization, and (iv) query execution.

atoms.statement: Query decomposition and source selection decomposes the federated query into subqueries and associates each with the data sources selected to execute it, with the candidate sources bounded by the data source descriptions given to the engine.

evidence.text: The query decomposition and source selection sub-problem decomposes the federated query into subqueries associated with data sources in the federation that are selected for executing the subqueries.
The number of data sources considered for selection are bounded by the data source description given to the federated query processing engine.

atoms.statement: Federated query engines use five join methods: nested loop join, bound-join, hash join, symmetric join, and multiple join; bound-join differs from nested loop join by executing the inner sub-query for a set of bindings rather than for every single binding of the outer intermediate results.

evidence.text: Five different join methods are used in federated query engines: nested loop join, bound-join, hash join, symmetric join, and multiple join [335].
Bound-join, like NLJ, executes inner sub-query for the set of bindings, unlike NLJ which executes the inner sub-query for every single binding of the intermediate results from the outer sub-query.

atoms.statement: Unlike distributed query processing systems, which have control over each dataset, federated query processing engines have no control over datasets in the federation, and data providers can join or leave the federation at any time and modify their datasets independently.

evidence.text: While distributed query processing systems have control over each dataset, federated query processing engines have no control over datasets in the federation and data providers can join or leave the federation at any time and modify their datasets independently.

atoms.statement: Finding an optimal federated query execution plan is computationally intractable; under a simplified cost function, minimizing cost for a query with many joins is proven NP-Complete.

evidence.text: Finding an optimal solution is computationally intractable [210].
Assuming a simplified cost function, it is proven that the minimization of this cost function for a query with many joins is NP-Complete.

atoms.statement: Cost-based optimization in federated settings is often not possible because data sources are autonomous and their descriptions may lack the needed statistics, so heuristic-based optimization, which uses minimal information from sources and properties of the query operators, can be used instead.

evidence.text: In federated settings, where data sources are autonomous, collecting such statistics might not always be possible.
Cost-based approaches are often not possible because the data source descriptions do not have the needed statistics.

Heuristic-based optimization techniques can be used to estimate the execution cost using minimum information collected from sources as well as the properties of the operators in the query, such as type of predicates, operators, etc. The output of the query planning and optimization is an optimized query, i.e., query execution plan, with operations (join, union) between subqueries.

atoms.statement: COMET is a context-aware RDF molecule matching framework that creates, identifies, and matches contextually equivalent RDF entities, merging entities that are equivalent according to a system-supplied context.

evidence.text: COMET is an entity matching framework designed to create, identify, and match contextually equivalent RDF entities.

Grounded on the entity matching component from the data integration technique proposed by Collarana et al. [84], we propose COMET, an entity matching approach to merge equivalent RDF entities based on context.

atoms.statement: In COMET, a context C is defined as any Boolean expression representing system criteria, i.e., a Boolean function that takes two RDF molecules M1 and M2 and returns true if they are similar according to the system context and false otherwise.

evidence.text: Context – We define a context C as any Boolean expression which represents the criteria of a system.
That is, C is a Boolean function that takes as input two molecules M1 and M2 and returns true if they are similar according to system context, and false otherwise.

atoms.statement: Two RDF molecules $M_G \in \Phi(G)$ and $M_D \in \Phi(D)$ are defined as contextually equivalent iff they satisfy the context, $C(M_1, M_2) = true$, and $Sim_f(M_G, M_D) = \max_{m \in \Phi(D)} Sim_f(M_G, m)$, i.e., they have the highest similarity value.

evidence.text: Then, MG and MD are defined as contextually equivalent iff
1. They are in the same context.
That is, C(M1, M2) = true 2.
They have the highest similarity value, i.e., Simf(MG, MD) = max(∀m∈Φ(D)Simf(MG, m))

atoms.statement: COMET works in two steps: it first computes similarity across RDF entities and uses Formal Concept Analysis to map contextually equivalent entities, then combines these results and runs a 1-1 perfect matching algorithm on the combined scores to synthesize a contextualized RDF graph.

evidence.text: of entity matching in RDF graphs in a context-aware manner: First, COMET computes the similarity measures across RDF entities and resorts to the Formal Concept Analysis algorithm to map contextually equivalent RDF entities.

Finally, COMET combines the results of the first step and executes a 1-1 perfect matching algorithm for matching RDF entities based on the combined scores to finally synthesize the matching into a contextualized RDF graph.

atoms.statement: COMET builds a bipartite graph between the molecule sets of the two RDF graphs, weighting edges by a user-supplied similarity function, and discards edges whose weights are lower than a threshold $\gamma$, so that $\gamma = 0.0$ keeps all edges and high thresholds such as 0.8 leave only a few.

evidence.text: The Dataset Partitioner employs a similarity function Simf and ontology O to compute the similarity between RDF molecules in φ(G) and φ(D) assigning the similarity score as vertices weight in the bipartite graph.
Thus, edges are discarded from the bipartite graph whose weights are lower than γ.
A threshold equal to 0.0 does not impose any restriction on the values of similarity; thus the bipartite graph includes all the edges.
High thresholds, e.g. 0.8, restrict the values of similarity, resulting in a bipartite graph comprising just a few edges.

atoms.statement: COMET validates context by replacing the attribute columns of an FCA binary matrix with the Boolean context condition C, so that FCA returns the formal concepts whose molecule sets satisfy the condition and the molecules or edges that do not meet it are pruned.

evidence.section: 4.5 Integration Use Case: Applying Fusion Policies
evidence.text: Instead of using attributes in the column of the FCA matrix, in our approach, we replace the attributes with a boolean condition C.

evidence.section: 4.5 Integration Use Case: Applying Fusion Policies
evidence.text: When applied to RDF molecules, formal concept analysis returns a set of formal concepts < M, C > where M is a set of all the molecules that contain all conditions contained in C.

evidence.section: 4.5 Integration Use Case: Applying Fusion Policies
evidence.text: Thus, the molecules that do not meet the context condition are pruned.

atoms.statement: COMET models context only as a Boolean function, so an entity is either valid or invalid within a context; the authors state that real-world context is more general and suggest probabilistic functions with range [0,1], for example via Probabilistic Soft Logic.

evidence.text: 1. Measuring context with probabilistic functions: In this chapter, we employ a straightforward definition of context conditions, i.e. modeling context as a Boolean function of entities.
According to this model, an entity is either valid within a context or invalid.
Meaning the range of the context function could be any value between the interval [0,1] instead of being only 0 or 1.
We suggest the use of Probabilistic Soft Logic (PSL) to implement this concept. 2.

atoms.statement: The authors state that the complexity of COMET's 1-1 matching algorithm is quadratic because COMET employs the original Formal Concept Analysis algorithm, and they suggest a distributed FCA version as a possible way to reduce run-time overhead.

evidence.text: In COMET, for example, the complexity of the 1-1 matching algorithm is quadratic as COMET employs the original Formal Concept Analysis algorithm.
As such, it is possible to evaluate a distributed version of the Formal Concept Analysis algorithm that may improve the run-time overhead in this work.

atoms.statement: In the experiments, COMET's precision and recall decrease as the number of highly similar molecules within the same context grows, and are perfect only in configuration A, where only one candidate is both highly similar and in context.

evidence.text: Moreover, the decrease in precision in recall of COMET with the increase of the number of highly similar molecules within the dataset also makes sense.
With a higher number of similar molecules to choose from, COMET has less of a chance of correctly identifying the perfect match.
On the other hand, in the case of configuration A, the precision and recall is perfect.
This is because the dataset in configuration A supplies only 1 perfect option (a highly similar molecule that also meets the context).

atoms.statement: Knowledge graph embedding models map the entities and relations of a knowledge graph, whose facts are triples $(h, r, t)$ of head, relation and tail, into a low-dimensional vector space.

evidence.text: For a Knowledge Graph with a set of triples in the form of (h, r, t) representing (head, relation, tail), KG embeddings aim at mapping entities and relations into a low-dimensional vector space.

atoms.statement: Knowledge graph embedding models can be roughly divided into three categories: translational and rotational models, semantic matching models, and neural network-based models.

evidence.text: Knowledge Graph embedding models can be roughly divided into three main categories:
– Translational and Rotational Based Models.

The score and loss function of these models optimize the vectors in a way that their plausibility is measured by the distance or degree of the entities with regard to the relation. – Semantic Matching Models.

atoms.statement: Knowledge graph embedding models obtain vector representations of entities and/or relations that are used in downstream tasks such as knowledge graph completion.

evidence.text: One of the most popular methods is Knowledge Graph Embedding models, which obtain the vector representation for entities and/or relations to be used in downstream tasks such as Knowledge Graph Completion tasks.

atoms.statement: Knowledge graph embedding models are described as a type of deductive reasoning in vector space that discovers new links, and their vectors are used in downstream tasks such as knowledge graph completion.

evidence.text: One of the most popular methods is Knowledge Graph Embedding models, which obtain the vector representation for entities and/or relations to be used in downstream tasks such as Knowledge Graph Completion tasks.
KGEs are a type of deductive reasoning in the vector space through discovery of new links.

atoms.statement: A knowledge graph embedding model defines a score function and a loss function to optimize the vectors, and the score function is trained over positive and negative samples to assign high scores to positive samples and low scores to negative samples.

evidence.text: Then, the KGE model defines a score and loss functions to further optimize the vectors through a specific embedding representation.
In these ways, the score function is trained over both the positive and negative samples and assigns a high score for positive samples and a low score to negative samples.
Each embedding model also has a loss function that optimizes the scoring.

atoms.statement: RotatE rotates the head embedding element-wise by a relation element of modulus 1 in complex space, so that $h_j \circ r_j = t_j$ holds for every element $j$ of a correct triple, which lets it encode symmetric, inverse and composition relation patterns.

evidence.text: Based on its score function, for every correct triple (h, r, t) there should be the relation of hjrj = tj which holds ∀j ∈{0, . . . , d}. hj, rj, tj are the j-th elements of the embedding vectors of h, r, t ∈Cd.

Re(rj)2 + Im(rj)2 = 1. The model performs a rotation of the j-th element hj of the head vector h by the j-th element rj = eiθrj of a relation vector r to get the j-th element tj of the tail vector t, where θrj is the phase of the relation r.
In this way, the RotatE model becomes capable of encoding symmetric, inverse, and composition relation patterns.

atoms.statement: LogicENN derives algebraic constraints for logical rules such as symmetric, inverse, transitive, negation, implication and equivalence from its score function and adds them as penalty terms to the loss function, which injects rules into learning.

evidence.text: Considering the formulation of the score function, the algebraic formulae (algebraic constraints) corresponding to each of the logical rules – namely symmetric, inverse, transitive, negation, implication, equivalence etc – are derived.
The formulae are then used as penalty terms to be added to the loss function for optimization.
This enables the injection of rules into the learning process of the network.

atoms.statement: DistMult cannot represent anti-symmetric relations because its score $h^T \mathrm{diag}(r) t$ equals $t^T \mathrm{diag}(r) h$, whereas ComplEx extends it to complex space so that $f_r(h,t) \neq f_r(t,h)$ and anti-symmetric relations can be modeled.

evidence.text: ComplEx ComplEx [430] is an extension of DistMult into the complex space.
Considering the scoring function of DistMult, it can be observed that it has a limitation in representing anti-symmetric relations since hT diag(r)t is equivalent to tT diag(r)h.
It is straightforward to show that fr(h, t) ̸= fr(t, h), i.e. ComplEx is capable of modeling anti-symmetric relations.

atoms.statement: TransE is limited in modeling 1-N, N-1 and N-M relations, and the source states that it cannot encode relations with reflexive and symmetric patterns.

evidence.text: However, TransE is limited in modeling 1-N, N-1 and N-M relations.
Due to this fact, encoding relations with reflexive and symmetric patterns becomes impossible, which is an important aspect in the inference of new knowledge.

atoms.statement: TransR can handle complex relations because it uses different vector spaces for entities and relations, but its computation is highly costly due to the high number of required parameters.

evidence.text: TransR is another KGE model that followed the basics from TranE as an extension of TransH with a difference that it encodes entities and relations in different vector spaces.
This model is capable of handling complex relations as it uses different spaces; however its computation is highly costly due to the high number of required parameters.

atoms.statement: The layered perspective, as chosen by the chapter's authors, combines three views of Knowledge Graphs (knowledge representation tools, knowledge management systems, and knowledge application services) as layers: representation of knowledge at the first layer, the management system for that knowledge in the middle, and the application it solves at the top.

evidence.text: The Layered Perspective. While these three views certainly have independent value, they are most interesting when put together as layers: on the first layer is the representation of knowledge, on the middle layer is the management system for this knowledge, and on the top layer the application that it solves.

atoms.statement: In the knowledge management systems view, the focus is the system that manages the Knowledge Graph, in the way database management systems play this role for databases.

evidence.text: – knowledge representation tools: where the focus is on how a Knowledge Graph is used to represent some form of knowledge. – knowledge management systems: where the focus is the system managing the Knowledge Graph, similar to how database management systems play this role for databases.

atoms.statement: In the knowledge application services view, the focus is on providing a layer of applications on top of a Knowledge Graph.

evidence.text: – knowledge application services: where the focus is on providing a layer of applications on top of a Knowledge Graph.

atoms.statement: Reasoning poses different requirements at each layer: at the representation layer it is a design consideration balancing expressive power against computational complexity, at the management layer a general-purpose reasoning (analogous to querying in an RDBMS) service is of utmost importance, and at the application layer the specific reasoning service the application requires or exposes is the focus.

evidence.text: – At the bottom-most layer (representation), reasoning is an important design consideration to achieve a good balance between expressive power and computational complexity. – At the middle layer (management), similar to a relational database management system, providing a general-purpose reasoning (or in a RDBMS: querying) service is of utmost importance. – At the top layer (application), the specific reasoning service required or exposed by the application becomes the focus.

atoms.statement: At the application layer, the specific reasoning service that the application requires or exposes becomes the focus.

evidence.text: – At the bottom-most layer (representation), reasoning is an important design consideration to achieve a good balance between expressive power and computational complexity. – At the middle layer (management), similar to a relational database management system, providing a general-purpose reasoning (or in a RDBMS: querying) service is of utmost importance. – At the top layer (application), the specific reasoning service required or exposed by the application becomes the focus.

atoms.statement: According to the authors, achieving a great overall KG system requires taking all layers and their interactions into account, because a good knowledge application platform is hardly possible if the knowledge representation layer is not fit for the purpose.

evidence.text: Of course, it is clear that to achieve a great overall system, all layers and their interactions have to be taken into account; it is hardly possibly to provide a good knowledge application platform if the knowledge representation layer is not fit for the purpose.

atoms.statement: The borders between the representation, management and application layers are fuzzy: many academic and industrial systems cover two or three of the layers, and representation tools can partly fulfill characteristics of management systems.

evidence.text: Interestingly, there is even another one, as the data management community often sees the management system in the middle as the focus. – The borders between these layers are fuzzy.
Many academic and industrial systems cover two or three of these layers.
In some cases, representation tools partly fulfill some of the characteristics of management systems.

atoms.statement: The order of the layers can be viewed in different ways: some communities see it top-down with the application as the focus, others bottom-up with knowledge representation as the focus, and the data management community often sees the middle management system as the focus.

evidence.text: – There are generally two ways of looking at the order of these layers.
Some communities tend to see it top-down with the application that the KG solves as the focus, others tend to see it as bottom-up, with the representation of knowledge as the focus.
Interestingly, there is even another one, as the data management community often sees the management system in the middle as the focus. – The borders between these layers are fuzzy.

atoms.statement: The authors regard the border between the management and application views as debatable: question answering and recommender systems would typically be considered application services, while entity resolution and link prediction are less clear and could be seen as requirements of a general-purpose knowledge management system.

evidence.text: Clearly, the border between the two views of management and application is debatable, and we invite the reader to critically think of what one should consider as an essential general-purpose service of a knowledge management system, and what should be part of an application service.

For example, while question answering in our opinion would typically be considered as an application service, as would be offering recommender system capabilities, it is less clear for relatively generalpurpose application services such as entity resolution and link prediction, which could be seen as a requirement of a general purporse knowledge management system.

atoms.statement: SANSA's DataLake component allows SPARQL to be used to query heterogeneous data sources, ranging from different databases to large files stored in HDFS to NoSQL stores.

evidence.text: DataLake. SANSA also has a DataLake component which allows it to query heterogeneous data sources ranging from different databases to large files stored in HDFS, to NoSQL stores, using SPARQL.

atoms.statement: In SANSA DataLake, a ParSet (Parallel dataSet) is a data structure that can be distributed and operated in parallel, and it follows a data model such as tables in tabular databases, graphs in graph databases, or documents in document databases.

evidence.text: ParSet, from Parallel dataSet, is a data structure that can be distributed and operated in parallel.
It follows certain data models, like tables in tabular databases, graphs in graph databases, or documents in a document database.

atoms.statement: In SANSA DataLake, the DEE (Distributed Execution Environment) is the shared physical space where ParSets can be transformed, aggregated and joined together.

evidence.text: DEE, from Distributed Execution Environment, is the shared physical space where ParSets can be transformed, aggregated and joined together.

atoms.statement: The Query Decomposor of SANSA DataLake splits the Basic Graph Pattern of a SPARQL query into star-shaped sub-BGPs, where each sub-BGP contains all the triple patterns that share the same subject variable.

evidence.text: It decomposes the query’s Basic Graph Pattern (BGP, conjunctive set of triple patterns in the where clause) into a set of star-shaped subBGPs, where each sub-BGP contains all the triple patterns sharing the same subject variable.

atoms.statement: In SANSA DataLake, the Data Wrapper generates exactly one ParSet for each identified star, and the ParSet is formed as a union when more than one entity is relevant to the star.

evidence.text: Each identified star from step (1) will generate exactly one ParSet.
If more than an entity is relevant, the ParSet is formed as a union.

atoms.statement: In SANSA DataLake's Distributed Query Processor, extracted ParSet join pairs are stored in an array. After the first pair is joined, each remaining pair is iterated and either joined or added to a queue; the queue is then iterated, with joined pairs unqueued, and the algorithm completes when the queue is empty.

evidence.text: After the first pair is joined, it iterates through each remaining pair to attempt further joins or, else, add to a queue.
Next, the queue is similarly iterated; when a pair is joined, it is unqueued.
The algorithm completes when the queue is empty.

atoms.statement: In SANSA DataLake, ParSets sometimes cannot be readily joined because of a syntactic mismatch between attribute values, and SANSA provides a method to correct these mismatches so that the joins become possible.

evidence.text: Sometimes ParSets cannot be readily joined due to a syntactic mismatch between attribute values; nevertheless, SANSA provides a method to correct these mismatches, thereby enabling the joins.

atoms.statement: Translating a SPARQL query into the query language of each relevant data source, as classical OBDA does, is in practice hard to achieve in highly heterogeneous Data Lake settings, so SANSA DataLake uses the DEE's query language as an intermediate query language.

evidence.text: Data Wrapper. In the classical OBDA, a SPARQL query has to be translated to the query language of the relevant data sources.
This is, in practice, hard to achieve in the highly heterogeneous Data Lake settings.
In our case, the intermediate query language is DEE’s query language, dictated by its internal data structure.

atoms.statement: SANSA DataLake requires wrappers that convert data entities from each source into the DEE's data structure, either fully or only partially when parts of the data can be pushed down to the original source.

evidence.text: There must exist wrappers to convert data entities from the source to DEE’s data structure, either fully or partially if parts of the data can be pushed down to the original source.

atoms.statement: SANSA DataLake currently supports CSV, Parquet files, Cassandra, MongoDB, Couchbase, ElasticSearch, and various JDBC sources such as MySQL and SQL Server.

evidence.text: SANSA DataLake currently supports CSV, Parquet files, Cassandra, MongoDB, Couchbase, ElasticSearch, and various JDBC sources e.g., MySQL, SQL Server.

atoms.statement: Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM), proposed by Hart, aims to give users appliance-level consumption information in a harmless way by disaggregating the aggregate consumption of an entire household, rather than installing meters throughout the household as Intrusive Load Monitoring would require.

evidence.text: Therefore, instead of the Intrusive Load Monitoring solution which influences users’ convenience, Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring was proposed by Hart in [183] with the main goal of providing users with the same information in a harmless way by aggregating entire household consumption at the appliance level, which can be seen in Fig. 1.

atoms.statement: Two main problems appear in the NILM literature: classification, which gives information about appliance activation, and regression, which estimates each appliance's individual consumption.

evidence.text: Having in mind the previous information, two main problems are present within the NILM literature - classification, which provides information about the activation on the appliance level, and regression for the estimation of the appliance’s individual consumption, as shown in the example Fig. 2.

atoms.statement: NILM was motivated by a cited conclusion that up to 12% of residential energy consumption can be decreased by giving users feedback on how energy has been used, that is, which appliances use how much electrical energy.

evidence.text: NILM was motivated by conclusions, such as those from [70], which claimed that up to 12% of residential energy consumption can be decreased by giving users feedback on how the energy has been used.
In other words, by providing the user with information about which of their appliances is using electrical energy and how much, significant savings can be reached.

atoms.statement: Hidden Markov Models suit NILM because they model processes with unobservable states, so individual appliance consumption can be estimated from the observable output, the aggregated consumption.

evidence.text: They were designed to model the processes with unobservable states, which is indeed the case with the NILM problem.
In other words, the goal is to estimate individual consumption in accordance with the observable output (aggregated consumption).

atoms.statement: Supervised NILM approaches are widely used, with neural networks the largest group, chiefly Recurrent Neural Networks (especially LSTM) and Convolutional Neural Networks (including Denoising Autoencoders), whose ability to extract complex features from input sequences was confirmed to increase prediction performance.

evidence.text: The biggest group currently popular in the literature is neural networks (NNs).
Their ability to extract complex features from an input sequence was confirmed to increase their final prediction performance.
Namely, two groups stood out to be most frequently used - Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) with the accent on Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) [302], and

atoms.statement: Unsupervised NILM techniques are widely applied because labeled data are unavailable for the houses in which services will be installed; examples include clustering and histogram analysis before conditional random fields, adaptation over unlabeled data, and single-channel source separation via Non Negative Matrix Factorization and Separation Via Tensor and Matrix Factorization.

evidence.text: The main cause of this is the fact that labeled data for the houses in which services are going to be installed are not available, as already discussed.
Therefore, many authors choose to use unsupervised learning techniques instead of improving generalization on the supervised ones.

Examples of these attempts are shown in [194] where clusterization and histogram analysis has been employed before using the conditional random fields approach, in [344] where adaptation over unlabeled data has been carried out in order to improve performance on the gaining houses, and in [136] where disaggregation was described as a single-channel source separation problem and Non Negative Matrix Factorization and Separation Via Tensor and Matrix Factorization were used.

atoms.statement: HMM-based NILM suffers from error propagation because an HMM presumes the current state depends on the previous one, so mistakes in estimating previous states significantly influence predictions of current states.

evidence.text: However, in all of the previously listed papers which cover the application of numerous HMM advancements to the NILM problem, the problem of error propagation is present.
Namely, as HMM presumes that a current state depends on a previous one, mistakes in estimating previous states have a significant influence on predicting current ones.

atoms.statement: Because NILM models would only be applied in houses without labeled data, and thus houses not used in training, validating results on a house whose measurements were used in training is considered inadequate, so an unseen house is set aside for validation and testing.

evidence.text: Additionally, it is obvious that the only application of the NILM models would be in houses which have not been used in the training phase, as they do not have labeled data (otherwise, there would be no need for NILM).
Bearing all of this in mind, validating the results from the data coming from the house whose measurements have already been used in the training process is considered inadequate.
Thus, it is accepted that for validation and testing purposes one, so called, unseen house is set aside and

atoms.statement: Generalization is even more crucial for NILM than in many other machine learning fields, because different houses may contain different types of the same appliance, so performance on a house not used in training may be significantly lower than the estimated one.

evidence.text: Even though the problem of achieving as high performance as possible on the testing rather than training domain is a hot topic in many fields of research within Machine Learning (ML) and Big Data, the generalization problem is even more crucial for NILM.

As different houses might include different types of the same appliances, the performance on the data coming from the house whose measurements have not been used in the training process might be significantly lower than the estimated one.

atoms.statement: Missing data is a problem in most NILM datasets whose severity varies by appliance: it can be neglected for cyclically operating refrigerators, but dropping activation sequences is unacceptable for washing machines, which are used about twice a week on average, making enough training data hard to collect.

evidence.text: The first one, present in most of the data sets, is the presence of the missing data.

For example, in the case of refrigerators, this is a minor problem which can be neglected because it works circularly, so each approximately 20 min it turns on or off, leading to numerous examples of both active and inactive working periods.

By contrast, when, for example, a washing machine is considered, dropping down the sequence of its activation is unacceptable as it is turned on twice a week in a household on average, so it is difficult to collect enough data for training purposes.

atoms.statement: Viewing a Knowledge Graph as a knowledge management system is analogous to a database management system for databases: a system to create, manipulate and retrieve data.

evidence.text: In this section, we present the view of Knowledge Graphs as knowledge management systems.
The clear analogy to see here is what a database management system is for databases: A system to create, manipulate and retrieve data.

atoms.statement: Bellomarini et al. define a knowledge graph as a semi-structured datamodel with three components: a ground extensional component (relational constructs for schema and data, modelable as graphs or generalizations), an intensional component (inference rules over the ground extensional constructs), and a derived extensional component produced by applying the rules to the ground component through reasoning.

evidence.text: “A semi-structured datamodel characterized by three components: (i) a ground extensional component, that is, a set of relational constructs for schema and data (which can be effectively modeled as graphs or generalizations thereof); (ii) an intensional component, that is, a set of inference rules over the constructs of the ground extensional component; (iii) a derived extensional component that can be produced as the result of the application of the inference rules over the ground extensional component (with the so-called “reasoning” process).” – Bellomarini et al., 2019 – [40].

atoms.statement: The management-system view adds to the knowledge-representation view the services that a Knowledge Graph as a knowledge management system has to offer.

evidence.text: What this adds to the previous section’s view of KGs as knowledge representation tools is the service that a KG as a knowledge management system has to offer.

atoms.statement: The desiderata for a Knowledge Graph Management System include high expressive power (at least as expressive as Datalog, i.e., full recursion), ontological reasoning (at least as expressive as SPARQL and OWL 2 QL), and low complexity (a core language tractable in data complexity).

evidence.text: The authors pose a number of requirements or desiderata for a Knowledge Graph Management System (KGMS) in terms of the main system capabilities:

– simple modular syntax: easy to add and remove facts and rules – high expressive power: at least as expressive as Datalog (i.e., full recursion) – numeric computation and aggregation: real-world required features – ontological reasoning: at least as expressive as SPARQL and OWL 2 QL – probabilistic reasoning: should support a form of probabilistic reasoning – low complexity: the core language should be tractable in data complexity – rule repository, management and ontology editor: management facilities – dynamic orchestration: allow orchestration of complex, real-world workflows

atoms.statement: A Knowledge Graph as a knowledge management system must support the user in adding knowledge to the KG, deriving new knowledge from existing knowledge, and retrieving data through a general-purpose query language.

evidence.text: In particular, it has to provide support for the user to (i) add knowledge to a KG (ii)
derive new knowledge using existing knowledge, and (iii) retrieve data through a form of general-purpose query language.

atoms.statement: The Vadalog system was presented in technical detail with a focus on algorithms and data structures that meet the requirements of high expressive power, ontological reasoning and low complexity at the same time.

evidence.text: They subsequently presented the Vadalog system [38] in more technical detail, focusing on algorithms and data structures to meet the requirement on high expressive power, ontological reasoning and low complexity at the same time.

atoms.statement: The authors consider question answering and recommender system capabilities typically to be application services, whereas general-purpose services such as entity resolution and link prediction are less clear, since they could be seen as requirements of a general-purpose knowledge management system.

evidence.text: For example, while question answering in our opinion would typically be considered as an application service, as would be offering recommender system capabilities, it is less clear for relatively generalpurpose application services such as entity resolution and link prediction, which could be seen as a requirement of a general purporse knowledge management system.

atoms.statement: The authors treat question answering, recommender systems, entity resolution and link prediction as application services because they offer a well-defined application, in contrast to a management system that offers a query language supporting such applications.

evidence.text: Here, we will consider all of four of these as application services as they clearly offer a well-defined application compared to a management system offering a query language that supports such applications.

atoms.statement: The source states that the border between the management view and the application-service view of KGs is debatable, and invites readers to consider what counts as an essential general-purpose service of a knowledge management system versus an application service.

evidence.text: Clearly, the border between the two views of management and application is debatable, and we invite the reader to critically think of what one should consider as an essential general-purpose service of a knowledge management system, and what should be part of an application service.

assessment_scope: Covers relaxed, acquire, release, acq_rel and seq_cst orderings as the book defines them: what each guarantees, how it constrains compiler/hardware reordering, which operations accept which orders, and device capability queries. Excludes memory_scope details, C++ memory_order::consume beyond its noted omission, and general memory-model theory outside the text.

atoms.statement: Under acquire-release ordering, one thread releasing an atomic variable and another thread acquiring the same atomic variable forms a synchronization point that guarantees any prior writes by the releasing thread are visible to the acquiring thread.

evidence.text: Under an acquire-release memory ordering, one thread releasing an

atomic variable and another thread acquiring the same atomic variable acts as a synchronization point between those two threads and guarantees that any prior writes to memory issued by the releasing thread are visible to the acquiring thread.

atoms.statement: Under a relaxed memory ordering, memory operations can be reordered without any restrictions, so memory_order::relaxed provides no ordering guarantees.

evidence.text: Under a relaxed memory ordering, memory operations can be
reordered without any restrictions.
There are no ordering guarantees.

atoms.statement: A memory ordering supplied to an atomic operation or fence tells the compiler what ordering guarantees are required for all other memory operations (to any address) relative to that operation, which constrains reordering by the compiler and hardware.

evidence.text: Supplying a memory order argument to an operation tells the compiler what memory ordering guarantees are required for all other memory operations (to any address) relative to that operation, as explained in the following:
By providing the compiler with information about our desired memory order, we can prevent reordering optimizations that are incompatible with the intended behavior of our applications.

atoms.statement: memory_order::acquire prevents read and write operations appearing after the operation in the program from being reordered before it, while memory_order::release prevents operations appearing before it from being reordered after it.

evidence.text: • memory_order::acquire
Read and write operations appearing after the operation in the program must occur after it (i.e., they cannot be reordered before the operation).

atoms.statement: Under a sequentially consistent memory ordering, the acquire-release guarantees still hold and there additionally exists a single global order of all atomic operations.

evidence.text: Under a sequentially consistent memory ordering, the guarantees
of acquire-release ordering still hold, but there additionally exists a single global order of all atomic operations.

atoms.statement: With memory_order::release, reads and writes appearing before the operation in the program cannot be reordered after it, and preceding writes are guaranteed visible to work-items synchronized by a corresponding acquire operation (an atomic using the same variable with memory_order::acquire, or a barrier function).

evidence.text: • memory_order::release

Read and write operations appearing before the operation in the program must occur before it (i.e., they cannot be reordered after the operation), and preceding write operations are guaranteed to be visible to other work-items which have been synchronized by a corresponding acquire operation (i.e., an atomic operation using the same variable and memory_order::acquire or a barrier function).

atoms.statement: Devices are required to support at least memory_order::relaxed for atomic operations, but fence operations must support at least relaxed, acquire, release, and acq_rel, a stronger minimum than for atomics.

evidence.text: All devices are required to support at least memory_order::relaxed.
All devices are required to support at least memory_order::relaxed, memory_order::acquire, memory_order::release, and memory_order::acq_rel.

Note that the minimum requirement for fences is stronger than the minimum requirement for atomic operations, since such fences are essential for reasoning about memory order in the presence of barriers.

atoms.statement: Load operations are incompatible with release semantics because they do not write values to memory, and store operations are incompatible with acquire semantics because they do not read values from memory.

evidence.text: Load operations do not write values to memory and are therefore
incompatible with release semantics.
Similarly, store operations do not read values from memory and are therefore incompatible with acquire semantics.

atoms.statement: A relaxed memory ordering cannot be used to implement a lock correctly, because lock-guarded memory updates rely on acquire-release ordering for protection from data races.

evidence.text: releasing the lock—only the lock variable is ever updated atomically, but we expect memory updates guarded by the lock to be protected from data races.
This behavior relies on an acquire-release memory ordering for correctness, and attempting to use a relaxed memory ordering to implement a lock will not work.

atoms.statement: Attempting to implement a lock with a relaxed memory ordering will not work, because lock correctness relies on acquire-release ordering to protect the memory updates guarded by the lock from data races.

evidence.text: releasing the lock—only the lock variable is ever updated atomically, but we expect memory updates guarded by the lock to be protected from data races.

assessment_scope: Covers what the book says about work-items, sub-groups and work-groups lacking guaranteed forward progress, how this affects barriers, cross-work-group synchronization and the device-wide latch, and the contrast with CUDA independent thread scheduling. Excludes formal progress-model theory not in the text.

source.title: Data Parallel C++, 2nd ed. (Reinders et al.), Apress 2023

atoms.statement: In SYCL basic data-parallel kernels, the execution model allows completely parallel execution of work-items but neither guarantees nor requires it, so items may run in any order, including sequentially on a single hardware thread.

evidence.text: allows for completely parallel execution but does not guarantee or require it.
Items can be executed in any order, including sequentially on a single hardware thread (i.e., without any parallelism)!

atoms.statement: Work-items within a work-group are scheduled so that they can cooperate, but they are not required to provide any specific forward progress guarantees, and executing them sequentially between barriers and collectives is a valid implementation.

evidence.text: Second, although the work-items in a work-group are scheduled

such that they can cooperate with one another, they are not required to provide any specific forward progress guarantees—executing the work-items within a work-group sequentially between barriers and collectives is a valid implementation.

atoms.statement: Work-items within a sub-group are not required to provide any specific forward progress guarantees, so an implementation may execute each work-item sequentially and switch between work-items only when a sub-group collective function is encountered.

evidence.text: Like work-groups, the work-items in a sub-group are not required to

provide any specific forward progress guarantees—an implementation is free to execute each work-item in a sub-group sequentially and only switch between work-items when a sub-group collective function is encountered.

atoms.statement: Communication and synchronization between work-items in the same work-group is guaranteed to be safe only when performed using the provided barrier and collective functions, and hand-coded synchronization routines may deadlock.

evidence.text: Communication and synchronization between work-items in the same work-group is only guaranteed to be safe when performed using the barrier and collective functions provided, and hand-coded synchronization routines may deadlock.

atoms.statement: A device-wide latch built on atomics requires that the device be able to execute all work-groups in the ND-range simultaneously with strong forward progress guarantees, so that the elected leaders of every work-group eventually reach the latch.

evidence.text: 3. The device must be capable of executing all work-
groups in the ND-­range simultaneously, with strong forward progress guarantees, in order to ensure that the elected leaders of every work-group in the NDrange eventually reach the latch.

atoms.statement: A device-wide latch built on atomics requires that the elected leader of each work-group make progress independently of the leaders in other work-groups, to avoid a single work-item spinning in the loop from starving other work-items that have yet to increment the counter.

evidence.text: 2. The elected leader of each work-group in the ND-
range must make progress independently of the leaders in other work-groups, to avoid a single work-item spinning in the loop from starving other work-items that have yet to increment the counter.

atoms.statement: CUDA devices with independent thread scheduling let individual threads make progress independently, so a syntactically correct SYCL program ported from CUDA may not execute correctly on all SYCL devices that lack such stronger forward progress guarantees.

evidence.text: For CUDA devices with independent thread scheduling, the individual
CUDA threads make progress independently, rather than as a group.
These additional forward progress guarantees enable code patterns to execute safely on a CUDA device that may not execute correctly on a SYCL device without the stronger forward progress guarantees.

atoms.statement: The memory ordering guarantees provided by atomics are orthogonal to forward progress guarantees, so relying on memory order alone to implement synchronization primitives may lead to deadlocks when forward progress guarantees are not sufficiently strong.

evidence.text: The memory ordering guarantees provided by atomics are orthogonal to forward progress guarantees, and, at the time of writing, work-group scheduling in SYCL is completely implementation-defined.
Relying on memory order alone to implement synchronization primitives may lead to deadlocks in the absence of sufficiently strong forward progress guarantees!

atoms.statement: On some devices all sub-groups within a work-group are guaranteed to eventually make progress, but this is currently implementation-defined behavior, so kernels that must remain portable cannot rely on sub-groups making progress.

evidence.text: However, on some devices, all sub-groups within a work-group are guaranteed to execute (make progress) eventually, which is a cornerstone
This is currently implementation-defined behavior, and so we cannot rely on sub-groups to make progress if we want our kernels to remain portable.

assessment_scope: Covers the atomic_ref class: non-owning semantics derived from C++20 std::atomic_ref, DefaultOrder/DefaultScope/address-space template arguments, use with buffers and USM, and the rule against mixing atomic and non-atomic access. Excludes the deprecated SYCL 1.2.1 atomic class except as contrast.

source.title: Data Parallel C++, 2nd ed. (Reinders et al.), Apress 2023

atoms.statement: Creating an atomic reference acts as a promise that the referenced variable will only be accessed atomically for the lifetime of that reference.

evidence.text: Creating an atomic reference effectively acts as a promise that the referenced variable will only be accessed atomically for the lifetime of the reference.

atoms.statement: In SYCL kernels, the atomic_ref class is based on C++20 std::atomic_ref, whose instances do not own their data but are constructed from an existing non-atomic variable.

evidence.text: The biggest difference between the two classes is that instances of std::atomic_ref do not own their data but are instead constructed from an existing non-atomic variable.
The atomic_ref class used in SYCL kernels is therefore based on std::atomic_ref.

atoms.statement: The SYCL atomic_ref class replaces the cl::sycl::atomic class from SYCL 1.2.1, which is deprecated in SYCL 2020, and the atomic_ref class should be used in its place.

evidence.text: The cl::sycl::atomic class is deprecated in SYCL 2020.
The
atomic_ref class (covered in the next section) should be used in its place.

atoms.statement: SYCL atomic_ref lets the programmer set the default memory order and memory scope as part of the object's type through the DefaultOrder and DefaultScope template arguments, as a compromise between C++ defaults and lowest-common-denominator defaults.

evidence.text: The design adopted by SYCL offers a compromise, allowing us to define our desired default behavior as part of an object’s type (using the DefaultOrder and DefaultScope template arguments).

Other orderings and scopes can be provided as runtime arguments to specific atomic operations as we see fit—the DefaultOrder and DefaultScope only impact operations where we do not or cannot override the default behavior (e.g., when using a shorthand operator like +=).

atoms.statement: DefaultOrder and DefaultScope affect only atomic_ref operations whose behavior is not or cannot be overridden, such as shorthand operators like +=, because other orderings and scopes can be passed as runtime arguments to specific operations.

evidence.text: Other orderings and scopes can be provided as runtime arguments to specific atomic operations as we see fit—the DefaultOrder and DefaultScope only impact operations where we do not or cannot override the default behavior (e.g., when using a shorthand operator like +=).

atoms.statement: Because atomic_ref wraps an existing non-atomic variable, non-atomic data can be created on the host, transferred to the device, and treated as atomic data only after the transfer.

evidence.text: These are exactly the semantics needed by SYCL, since they allow us to create non-atomic data on the host, transfer that data to the device, and treat it as atomic data only after it has been transferred.

atoms.statement: To use atomic operations with buffers in SYCL, a buffer of non-atomic data is created and transferred to the device, and that data is then accessed through an atomic reference.

evidence.text: To use atomic operations in conjunction with buffers, we must create a buffer of non-atomic data to be transferred to the device and then access that data through an atomic reference.

atoms.statement: While any atomic_ref referencing a specific object exists, all accesses to that object must occur atomically via an instance of atomic_ref.

evidence.text: When mixing atomic and non-atomic accesses like this, it is important to pay attention to object lifetimes—while any atomic_ref referencing a specific object exists, all accesses to that object must occur (atomically) via an instance of atomic_ref.

atoms.statement: Unlike atomic_ref, std::atomic cannot be used in SYCL device kernels because its instances own their data and cannot be moved or copied, so atomic objects cannot be created on the host and transferred to the device; attempting to use it in a kernel causes a compiler error.

evidence.text: Instances of the atomic class own their data, cannot be moved or copied, and can only be updated using atomic operations.
Unfortunately, they also prevent the class from being used in SYCL kernels—it is impossible to create atomic objects on the host and transfer them to the device!
We are free to continue using std::atomic in our host code, but attempting to use it inside of device kernels will result in a compiler error.

atoms.statement: Atomicity guarantees do not apply if only some of the concurrent accesses to a memory location use atomics, and mixing atomic and non-atomic operations on the same location at the same time results in undefined behavior.

evidence.text: Note that this guarantee does not apply if only some of the accesses use atomics and that it is our responsibility as programmers to ensure that we do not concurrently access the same data using operations with different atomicity guarantees.
Mixing atomic and non-atomic operations on the same memory location(s) at the same time results in undefined behavior!

assessment_scope: Covers RAW, WAR and WAW dependences (and RAR as non-constraining) as expressed through accessors in the task graph DAG, and what they imply for ordering and data movement. Excludes event-based and in-order queue mechanisms except as contrast.

source.title: Data Parallel C++, 2nd ed. (Reinders et al.), Apress 2023

atoms.statement: A Read-after-Write (RAW) dependence occurs when one task needs to read data produced by a different task, and it describes the flow of data between the two kernels.

evidence.text: The first, Read-after-Write (RAW), occurs when one task needs to read data produced by a different task.
This type of dependence describes the flow of data between two kernels.

atoms.statement: A Write-after-Read (WAR) dependence occurs when one task needs to update data after another task has read it, and it is also called an anti-dependence.

evidence.text: The second type of dependence happens when one task needs to update data after another task has read it.
We call that type of dependence a Write-after-Read (WAR) dependence.
WAR dependences are also called anti-dependences.

atoms.statement: A Write-after-Write (WAW) dependence occurs when two tasks try to write the same data, and it is also called an output dependence.

evidence.text: The final type of data dependence occurs when two tasks try to write the same data.
This is known as a Write-after-Write (WAW) dependence.
The WAW dependence, also called an output dependence, ensures that the final output will be correct on the host.

atoms.statement: In a task graph, which is a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are tasks and whose edges are dependences, the edges are one-way because a dependence means task A must happen before task B.

evidence.text: This task graph is specifically a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where the nodes are the tasks and the edges are the dependences.
The graph is directed because dependences are one-way: task A must happen before task B.
The graph is acyclic because it cannot contain any cycles or paths from a node that lead back to itself.

atoms.statement: A RAW dependence between a kernel and the host, arising because the host wants to read a buffer after the kernel has finished, forces the runtime to copy that buffer back to the host.

evidence.text: Finally, we also create a RAW dependence on buffer c_buf between kernel computeC and the host since the host wants to read C after the kernel has finished.
This forces the runtime to copy buffer c_buf back to the host.

atoms.statement: RAW dependences ensure that data flows in the correct direction between computations, while WAR dependences ensure that existing values are not overwritten before they are read.

evidence.text: RAW dependences ensure that data properly flows in the correct direction, while WAR dependences ensure existing values are not overwritten before they are read.

atoms.statement: A Read-after-Read (RAR) scenario, where two kernels only read the same buffer through read-only accessors, places no extra restrictions on the runtime, so the kernels are free to execute in any order, including at the same time.

evidence.text: kernel readA is submitted after kernel computeB, this creates a Read-after-Read (RAR) scenario.
However, RARs do not place extra restrictions on the runtime, and the kernels are free to execute in any order.
Indeed, a runtime might prefer to execute kernel readA before kernel computeB or even execute both at the same time.

atoms.statement: Even if a kernel only writes to a buffer, the buffer's original content may still be moved to the device, because there is no guarantee that the kernel will write all values in the buffer.

evidence.text: even if a kernel will only write to a buffer, the original content of the buffer may still be moved to the device because there is no guarantee that all values in the buffer will be written by a kernel (see Chapter 7 for tags that let us optimize in these cases).

atoms.statement: SYCL graphs ensure correct execution only based on the dependences that have been expressed, so the programmer is responsible for making sure the graph correctly expresses all dependences in the program.

evidence.text: No matter which types of graph a computation needs, SYCL graphs ensure that a program will execute correctly based on the expressed dependences.
However, it is up to the programmer to make sure that a graph correctly expresses all the dependences in a program.

assessment_scope: Covers the reduction function and reducer class, scalar vs array reductions, result-availability and access restrictions, identity values for user-defined reductions, and implementation-defined return type. Excludes hand-written reduction kernels beyond contrast.
