atoms.statement: The SYCL reduction library provides an abstraction for describing variables with reduction semantics, so that programmers need not maintain their own libraries of portable and highly performant reduction kernels.

evidence.text: Rather than require that each of us maintain our own library of portable and highly performant reduction kernels, SYCL provides a convenient abstraction for describing variables with reduction semantics.

atoms.statement: The SYCL reduction abstraction makes explicit that a reduction is being performed, which allows an implementation to select among different reduction algorithms for different combinations of device, data type, and reduction operation.

evidence.text: This abstraction simplifies the expression of reduction kernels and makes the fact that a reduction is being performed explicit, allowing implementations to select between different reduction algorithms for different combinations of device, data type, and reduction operation.

atoms.statement: A reduction initialized with a buffer or a USM pointer is a scalar reduction operating on the first object in an array, whereas a reduction initialized with a span is an array reduction.

evidence.text: If a reduction is initialized using a buffer or a USM pointer, the
reduction is a scalar reduction, operating on the first object in an array.

atoms.statement: Each component of an SYCL array reduction is independent, so an array reduction on an array of size $N$ is equivalent to $N$ scalar reductions with the same data type and operator.

evidence.text: Each component of an array reduction is independent—we can think of an array reduction operating on an array of size N as equivalent to N scalar reductions with the same data type and operator.

atoms.statement: A SYCL reduction initialized with a buffer or a USM pointer is a scalar reduction operating on the first object in an array, whereas a reduction initialized with a span is an array reduction.

evidence.text: If a reduction is initialized using a buffer or a USM pointer, the
reduction is a scalar reduction, operating on the first object in an array.
If a reduction is initialized using a span, the reduction is an array reduction.

atoms.statement: Every SYCL reducer provides a combine() function that combines the partial result from a single work-item with the value of the reduction variable, and its behavior is implementation-defined.

evidence.text: Specifically, every reducer provides a combine() function which
combines the partial result (from a single work-item) with the value of the reduction variable.
How this combine function behaves is implementation-defined but is not something that we need to worry about when writing a kernel.

atoms.statement: The result of a SYCL reduction is not guaranteed to be written back to the original variable until the kernel has completed.

evidence.text: The result of a reduction is not guaranteed to be written back to
the original variable until the kernel has completed.

atoms.statement: SYCL implementations can automatically determine the correct identity value only when the reduction operates on simple arithmetic types and uses one of several standard function objects such as plus, so user-defined reductions may improve performance by specifying the identity value directly.

evidence.text: SYCL implementations can only automatically determine the correct
identity value to use when a reduction is operating on simple arithmetic types and the reduction operator is one of several standard function objects (e.g., plus).
For user-defined reductions (i.e., those operating on user-defined types and/or using user-defined function objects), we may be able to improve performance by specifying the identity value directly.

atoms.statement: Unlike reduction abstractions in other languages, the SYCL reduction library forbids inspecting intermediate values of a reduction variable during kernel execution and forbids updating it with anything other than the specified combination function.

evidence.text: One important way in which the SYCL reduction library differs from

reduction abstractions found in other languages is that it restricts our access to the reduction variable during kernel execution—we cannot inspect the intermediate values of a reduction variable, and we are forbidden from updating the reduction variable using anything other than the specified combination function.

assessment_scope: Covers device, host and shared allocations: accessibility, migration behavior, data movement implications, required allocation parameters (context, device), and restricted vs on-demand migration. Excludes allocator syntax styles and prefetch/mem_advise details.

atoms.statement: A USM device allocation resides in device-attached memory (such as (G)DDR or HBM), can be read and written by kernels running on a specific device, but cannot be directly accessed from host code.

evidence.text: This first type of allocation is what we need in order to have a pointer into a device’s attached memory, such as (G)DDR or HBM.
Device allocations can be read from or written to by kernels running on a specific device, but they cannot be directly accessed from code executing on the host (and usually not by devices either).

atoms.statement: A USM host allocation is made in host memory and is accessible on both the host and the device, so the same pointer value is valid in host code and in device kernels.

evidence.text: A host allocation occurs in host memory that is accessible both on the
host and on a device. This means the same pointer value is valid both in host code and in device kernels.

atoms.statement: A USM shared allocation is accessible on both host and device like a host allocation, but differs in that it is free to migrate automatically between host memory and device-attached memory without programmer intervention.

evidence.text: Like host allocations, shared allocations are accessible on both the host and device.
The difference between them is that shared allocations are free to migrate between host memory and device-attached memory, automatically, without our intervention.

atoms.statement: USM device allocations require explicit data movement, performed by enqueueing memcpy() operations found in the queue and handler classes to transfer data between host and device, whereas host and shared allocations provide implicit data movement.

evidence.text: Device allocations require us to explicitly move data between host and device, while host and shared allocations provide implicit data movement.
Explicit data movement with USM is accomplished with device allocations and a special memcpy() found in the queue and handler classes.
We enqueue memcpy() operations (actions) to transfer data either from the host to the device or from the device to the host.

atoms.statement: When a host allocation is accessed from a device, its data does not migrate to device-local memory but is typically sent over a bus such as PCI Express that connects the device to the host.

evidence.text: However, when such a pointer is accessed, the data always comes from host memory.
If it is accessed on a device, the
data does not migrate from the host to device-local memory.
Instead, data is typically sent over a bus, such as PCI Express (PCI-E), that connects the device to the host.

atoms.statement: Once a USM shared allocation has migrated to device-local memory, device accesses come from much faster local memory instead of remotely accessing host memory through a higher-latency connection, and this migration is typically performed by runtime and driver mechanisms hidden from the programmer.

evidence.text: this regard, it is very similar to a host allocation, but it differs in that data can now migrate between host memory and device-local memory.
This means that accesses on a device, after the migration has occurred, happen from much faster device-local memory instead of remotely accessing host memory though a higher-latency connection.
Typically, this is accomplished through mechanisms inside the runtime and lower-level drivers that are hidden from us.

atoms.statement: If a device cannot migrate shared allocations on demand, the runtime must conservatively assume a kernel might access any allocation in device-attached memory, so the host and device should not access a shared allocation at the same time and applications should alternate access in phases.

evidence.text: If a device cannot migrate memory on demand, that means the runtime must be conservative and assume that a kernel might access any allocation in its device-attached memory.
First, it means that the host and device should not try to access a
shared allocation at the same time.
Applications should instead alternate access in phases.

atoms.statement: If a device cannot migrate memory on demand, shared allocations are limited by the total memory attached to the device, whereas a device supporting on-demand migration can oversubscribe its attached memory, possibly with a performance penalty from extra data movement.

evidence.text: that allocations are limited by the total amount of memory attached to a device.
If a device cannot migrate memory on demand, it cannot migrate data to the host to make room to bring in different data.

If a device does support on-demand migration, it is possible to oversubscribe its attached memory, allowing a kernel to compute on more data than the device’s memory could normally contain, although this flexibility may come with a performance penalty due to extra data movement.

atoms.statement: Although shared allocations can migrate, not all SYCL implementations necessarily migrate them; some devices may implement them identically to host allocations, so they remain visible on host and device but may not show the performance gains of migration.

atoms.statement: In SYCL, a sub-group is an implementation-defined subset of the work-items in a work-group that execute together on the same hardware resources or with additional scheduling guarantees.

evidence.text: A sub-­

assessment_scope: Covers SYCL asynchronous errors: why they are decoupled from host execution, the asynchronous handler, registration on queues/contexts, the exact invocation points, and default behavior. Excludes synchronous exception handling and error management strategy in general C++.

atoms.statement: In SYCL, asynchronous errors are errors detected by the SYCL runtime (or an underlying backend) that occur independently of the execution of commands in the host program.

evidence.text: Asynchronous errors are detected by the SYCL runtime (or an underlying backend), and the errors occur independently of execution of commands in the host program.

atoms.statement: In SYCL, asynchronous errors arise because some errors occur on a device or when launching work on a device, and such errors are typically decoupled in time from the host program's execution, so they do not integrate cleanly with regular C++ exception handling.

evidence.text: Heterogeneous programming requires an additional level of error management beyond this because some errors occur on a device or when trying to launch work on a device.
These errors are typically decoupled in time from the host program’s execution, and as such they don’t integrate cleanly with regular C++ exception handling mechanisms.

atoms.statement: In SYCL, the asynchronous handler is a function defined by the application and registered with SYCL contexts and/or queues, which the SYCL runtime invokes with a list of unprocessed asynchronous exceptions.

evidence.text: The asynchronous handler is a function that the application defines, which is registered with SYCL contexts and/or queues.

At the times defined by the next section, if there are any unprocessed asynchronous exceptions that are available to be handled, then the asynchronous handler is invoked by the SYCL runtime and passed a list of these exceptions.

atoms.statement: The SYCL runtime invokes the asynchronous handler only at five points: when the host calls queue::throw_asynchronous() or queue::wait_and_throw() on a specific queue, when the host calls event::wait_and_throw() on a specific event, when a queue is destroyed, or when a context is destroyed.

evidence.text: The asynchronous handler is instead called at the following very specific times:
1. When the host program calls queue::throw_
2. When the host program calls queue::wait_and_
3. When the host program calls event::wait_and_
4. When a queue is destroyed
5. When a context is destroyed

atoms.statement: If no asynchronous handler is supplied, the default handler should display information about the errors in the exception list and then end the application through std::terminate, which should cause the operating system to report abnormal termination.

evidence.text: The default handler should display some information to the user on
any errors in the exception list and then will end the application through std::terminate, which should cause the operating system to report that termination was abnormal.

atoms.statement: SYCL stores asynchronous errors in lists internal to the runtime and releases them for processing only at specific points that the programmer can control.

evidence.text: The errors are stored in lists internal to the SYCL
runtime and only released for processing at specific points that the programmer can control.

atoms.statement: Relying on error detection during program teardown does not work in all cases; for example, if a program terminates only when a convergence criterion is met that requires successful device kernel execution, an asynchronous exception may mean convergence never occurs and teardown, where the error would be noticed, is never reached.

evidence.text: Relying on error detection during program teardown doesn’t work

in all cases, though. For example, if a program will only terminate when some algorithm convergence criteria are achieved and if those criteria are only achievable by successful execution of device kernels, then an asynchronous exception may signal that the algorithm will never converge and begin the teardown (where the error would be noticed).

atoms.statement: SYCL disallows C++ exception handling mechanisms such as throw within device code because of performance costs on some types of devices, so errors detected in device code must be signaled by non-exception techniques such as writing to an error-log buffer or returning a designated invalid result.

evidence.text: SYCL explicitly disallows C++ exception handling mechanisms (such
as throw) within device code, because there are performance costs for some types of devices that we usually don’t want to pay.
If we detect that something has gone wrong within our device code, we should signal the error using existing non-exception-based techniques.

atoms.statement: SYCL does not report asynchronous errors immediately as they occur because immediate reporting would make error management and safe (particularly multithreaded) programming more difficult and expensive, for example through additional host-device synchronizations.

evidence.text: Errors aren’t reported immediately as they occur because management of errors and safe application programming (particularly multithreaded) would become more difficult and expensive (e.g., additional synchronizations between host and device) if that was the case.

atoms.statement: The authors advise that unless error management principles allow recovery of a known program state and confidence that continuing is safe, an asynchronous handler should terminate the application, because merely printing a message and returning risks incorrect results from a program that continued despite a detected error.

evidence.text: Although it’s up to us to decide what an asynchronous handler does
internally, a common mistake is to print an error message (that may be missed in the noise of other messages from the program), followed by completion of the handler function.
This reduces the chance that incorrect results will appear from a program where an error was detected, but where the application was inadvertently allowed to continue with execution regardless.

atoms.statement: Quasi-isometric spaces are known to share properties such as volume growth, isoperimetric inequalities, and Liouville-type theorems, but most of these connections require additional conditions on local geometry, typically bounded geometry for manifolds and bounded geometry/controlled weights for graphs.

evidence.text: Kanai. It is well known in context with Riemannian manifolds and (combinatorial) graphs that quasi-isometric spaces share many important properties: e.g., geometric properties (such as volume growth and isoperimetric inequalities) [122], parabolicity/transience [47, 122, 160], Nash inequalities [47], Liouville-type theorems for harmonic functions of finite energy [47, 106, 107, 151,160,194] and parabolic/elliptic Harnack inequalities [14,15,47,103].
However, we stress that most of these connections also require additional conditions on the local geometry of the spaces.
Typically, one imposes a bounded geometry assumption for manifolds [122] and bounded geometry/controlled weights assumptions for graphs [12,15], [195, Chapter VII].

In such tissues, the unopposed hydrostatic pressure difference ensures that only transendothelial fluid filtration occurs.

atoms.statement: The ROSE concept describes four dynamic fluid phases of fluid therapy: resuscitation, optimization, stabilization and evacuation.

evidence.text: 4 phases: The four dynamic fluid phases are: resuscitation, optimization, stabilization
and evacuation.

atoms.statement: The ROSE concept is presented as a framework for avoiding fluid overload.

evidence.text: Table 8.5 The ROSE concept avoiding fluid overload (adapted from Malbrain et al. with permission [28])

atoms.statement: In the ROSE concept, the four phases are distinguished by time frame: resuscitation occurs over minutes, optimization over hours, stabilization over days, and evacuation over days to weeks.

evidence.text: Time frame Minutes Hours Days Days to weeks

atoms.statement: In the ROSE concept, the resuscitation phase follows the first hit (for example sepsis, burns, pancreatitis or trauma), and the patient enters the "ebb" phase of shock, which occurs within minutes and is characterized by low mean arterial pressure and microcirculatory impairment.

evidence.text: After the first hit which can be sepsis (but also burns, pancreatitis, or trauma), the patient will enter the “ebb” phase of shock.

This phase of severe circulatory shock, that can be life-threatening, occurs within minutes and is characterized by a low mean arterial pressure and microcirculatory impairment and can be accompanied with high cardiac output (hyperdynamic circulatory shock) or low cardiac output (e.g., septic shock with severe hypovolemia or septic shock with cardiomyopathy).

atoms.statement: In the optimization phase of the ROSE concept, the second hit (ischemia and reperfusion) occurs within hours, and the phase addresses the question of when to stop fluid therapy in order to avoid the risk of fluid overload.

evidence.text: The second hit occurs within hours and refers to ischemia and reperfusion.
In this phase, we try to find an answer to the second question: “When to stop fluid therapy?”, avoiding potential risks of fluid administration (fluid overload).

atoms.statement: In the ROSE concept, the resuscitation phase addresses the question "When to start fluid therapy?", weighing the benefits of fluid resuscitation, namely restoration of organ perfusion.

evidence.text: In this phase, we try to find an answer to the first question: “When to start fluid therapy?”, addressing the benefits of fluid resuscitation (restoration of organ perfusion).

atoms.statement: In the ROSE optimization phase, the question addressed is "When to stop fluid therapy?", with the aim of avoiding the potential risks of fluid administration (fluid overload).

evidence.text: In this phase, we try to find an answer to the second question: “When to stop fluid therapy?”, avoiding potential risks of fluid administration (fluid overload).

atoms.statement: In the ROSE stabilization phase, fluid therapy is used only for ongoing maintenance and replacement of fluid losses, which may include rehydration if unresolved pathologic conditions cause ongoing losses.

evidence.text: Fluid therapy is now only used for ongoing maintenance and replacement fluids either in setting of normal fluid losses (i.e., renal, gastrointestinal, insensible), but this could also be fluid infusion (including rehydration) if the patient was experiencing ongoing losses because of unresolved pathologic conditions [28, 57].

atoms.statement: In the evacuation phase of the ROSE concept, the goal is late goal-directed fluid removal (de-resuscitation), achieved by reversing the positive fluid balance either spontaneously or actively.

evidence.text: Late goal-directed fluid removal (de-resuscitation)
Reversal of the positive fluid balance, either spontaneous or active

atoms.statement: In the ROSE concept, the stabilization phase is distinguished from the resuscitation and optimization phases by the absence of shock (compensated or uncompensated) or of an imminent threat of shock.

evidence.text: However, this stage is distinguished from the prior two by the absence of shock (compensated or uncompensated) or the imminent threat of shock.

atoms.statement: In the evacuation phase of the ROSE concept, the main risk is excessive fluid removal, which may induce hypotension, hypoperfusion, and a "fourth hit".

evidence.text: Excessive fluid removal, possibly inducing hypotension, hypoperfusion, and a “fourth hit”

atoms.statement: In the resuscitation phase of the ROSE concept, early adequate fluid management is described as lifesaving, but its goal should be individualized for each patient, taking the patient's premorbid conditions into account.

evidence.text: Early adequate fluid management is not only useful but also lifesaving in this phase, but the goal should be individualized for every patient; also considering the patient’s premorbid conditions [1, 58–60].

atoms.statement: Late Goal-Directed Fluid Removal (LGFR), also called de-resuscitation, is defined as active fluid removal with diuretics or renal replacement therapy with net ultrafiltration, started within the first week of ICU stay.

evidence.text: Definitions and Key Messages • Late Goal-Directed Fluid Removal (LGFR) is defined as active fluid removal
with diuretics or renal replacement therapy with net ultrafiltration and started within the first week of ICU stay also referred to as de-resuscitation

atoms.statement: Late Conservative Fluid Management (LCFM) is defined as 2 consecutive days of negative fluid balance within the first week of the ICU stay, and describes a moderate fluid management strategy after the initial early adequate fluid management to avoid or reverse fluid overload.

evidence.text: Late Conservative Fluid Management (LCFM) describes a moderate fluid management strategy following the initial EAFM in order to avoid (or reverse) fluid overload.
Definitions and Key Messages • Late Conservative Fluid Management (LCFM) is defined as 2 consecutive days
of negative fluid balance within the first week of the ICU stay.

atoms.statement: De-resuscitation is defined as a strategy of actively and forcefully removing accumulated fluid, in an otherwise hemodynamically stable patient with clinical evidence of fluid overload, in order to treat or prevent end-organ damage from fluid overload without producing hypovolemia and organ ischemia.

evidence.text: De-resuscitate when necessary: De-resuscitation is a strategy to remove accu­
mulated fluid forcefully, in an otherwise hemodynamically stable patient with clinical evidence of fluid overload.
The aim of de-resuscitation is to treat and/or prevent end-organ damage resulting from fluid overload without producing hypovolemia and organ ischemia.

atoms.statement: In a randomized trial of hemodynamically stable, hypoproteinemic mechanically ventilated ARDS patients, adding 20% albumin boluses to furosemide for 72 hours produced a larger negative fluid balance, fewer hypotension episodes and significantly improved oxygenation compared with furosemide plus placebo.

evidence.text: In an elegant study, Greg Martin et al. randomized hemodynamically stable, hypoproteinemic patients who are on mechanical ventilator for ARDS to either furosemide with albumin (100 ml boluses of 20% albumin every 8-h) or furosemide with placebo for 72 h [16].
Addition of albumin was shown to produce larger negative fluid balance and lesser episodes of hypotension, in addition to a significant improvement in oxygenation.

atoms.statement: The PAL strategy (PEEP matched to intra-abdominal pressure, plus albumin, plus furosemide or ultrafiltration) was associated, in a pilot study, with greater negative fluid balance and greater reduction in extravascular lung water index and intra-abdominal pressure than in control subjects, with improved oxygenation and shorter ICU stay and without compromising cardiovascular or renal function.

evidence.text: –– Addition of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) matching intra-abdomi­

nal pressure (IAP), in addition to albumin plus diuretics (or ultrafiltration) (PAL strategy—PEEP, albumin and lasix or furosemide), had shown to be associated with greater negative fluid balance and greater reduction in extravascular lung water index (EVLWI) and IAP compared to control subjects [17].
PAL strategy also showed improved clinical outcomes (improved oxygenation, shorter ICU length of stay) without compromising cardiovascular or renal function.

atoms.statement: Active fluid removal in de-resuscitation can be achieved either by judicious use of diuretics or by ultrafiltration using continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) or slow low efficiency hemodialysis (SLED).

evidence.text: • How to initiate? Active removal of fluid can be achieved either by judicious use
of diuretics or by ultrafiltration [continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) or slow low efficiency hemodialysis (SLED)].

atoms.statement: De-resuscitation should be stopped when hemodynamic instability or obvious hypovolemia occurs, in which case fluid removal is suspended and fluid may be judiciously re-administered, and removal may be restarted at a lower rate once hypovolemia or hypoperfusion is mitigated.

evidence.text: –– Hemodynamic instability or obvious evidence of hypovolemia; in which case,
fluid removal must be suspended and fluid may be re-administered judiciously.
Fluid removal may be re-initiated at a lower rate, once hypovolemia or hypoperfusion is mitigated [12].

atoms.statement: De-resuscitation should be considered only when the patient is hemodynamically stable on no or minimal vasopressor dose, needs no additional fluid boluses and has no ongoing fluid loss requiring replacement, and has clinical and objective evidence of fluid overload with reasonable suspicion of organ damage directly resulting from fluid accumulation.

evidence.text: • When to start? Patient must be hemodynamically stable on no or minimal dose
of vasopressors before considering de-resuscitation.
He or she should not be requiring additional boluses or fluid or there should not be any ongoing fluid loss requiring replacement.
Clinical and objective evidence of fluid overload should be present with reasonable suspicion of organ damage (or impending one) directly resulting from the fluid accumulation.

atoms.statement: De-resuscitation is an active fluid removal to treat fluid accumulation causing organ dysfunction, whereas de-escalation means discontinuing or reducing IV fluids to prevent fluid accumulation.

evidence.text: De-escalation means discontinuation or reducing IV fluids to prevent fluid accumulation.
De-resuscitation is an active fluid removal to treat fluid accumulation causing organ dysfunction.

atoms.statement: According to the Abdominal Compartment Society (WSACS), intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) is defined as a sustained increase in intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) equal to or greater than 12 mmHg.

evidence.section: Intra-abdominal Hypertension and Abdominal Compartment Syndrome
evidence.text: According to the Abdominal Compartment Society (WSACS, www.wsacs.org), intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) is defined as a sustained increase in IAP equal to or greater than 12 mmHg [1].

atoms.statement: Abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) is defined as a sustained increase in IAP above 20 mmHg that is associated with new organ dysfunction or failure.

evidence.section: Intra-abdominal Hypertension and Abdominal Compartment Syndrome
evidence.text: Abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) is defined as a sustained increase in IAP above 20 mmHg that is associated with new organ dysfunction/failure.

atoms.statement: IAH is graded by IAP: grade I is 12 to 15 mmHg, grade II is 15 to 20 mmHg, grade III is 20 to 25 mmHg, and grade IV is above 25 mmHg.

evidence.section: Intra-abdominal Hypertension and Abdominal Compartment Syndrome
evidence.text: IAH is graded as follows: grade I between 12 and 15 mmHg, grade II between 15 and 20 mmHg, grade III between 20 and 25 mmHg, and grade IV are IAP values above 25 mmHg.

atoms.statement: Abdominal perfusion pressure (APP) is calculated by subtracting IAP from mean arterial pressure, $APP = MAP - IAP$, and ideally should be higher than 60 mmHg.

evidence.section: Intra-abdominal Hypertension and Abdominal Compartment Syndrome
evidence.text: The abdominal perfusion pressure (APP), ideally a value higher than 60 mmHg, is calculated by subtracting the IAP from the mean arterial pressure (MAP).

atoms.statement: The filtration gradient is defined as glomerular filtration pressure minus proximal tubular pressure, which equals $MAP - 2 \times IAP$.

evidence.text: The Filtration Gradient (FG) = glomerular filtration pressure (GFP) − proximal tubular pressure (PTP) = MAP – 2 × IAP [11].

atoms.statement: Large-volume fluid administered to restore hemodynamic stability may result in secondary IAH and ACS, and elevated IAP in turn stimulates antidiuretic hormone, further promoting fluid retention.

evidence.text: state similar to sepsis. To restore hemodynamic stability, fluid resuscitation is often the first choice.
However, administering large amounts of fluids may result in secondary IAH and ACS.
The increased IAP stimulates anti-diuretic hormone (ADH), further promoting fluid retention [7] as well as renin-angiotensin-aldosterone release [8].

atoms.statement: Primary IAH originates from injury or disease within the abdominopelvic cavity (e.g., ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, bowel perforation, spleen rupture), whereas secondary IAH results from conditions of extra-abdominal origin (e.g., sepsis, major burns, or other conditions requiring massive fluid resuscitation).

evidence.section: Intra-abdominal Hypertension and Abdominal Compartment Syndrome
evidence.text: Primary IAH originates from injury or disease within the abdominopelvic cavity (e.g., a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, bowel perforation and spleen rupture), whereas secondary IAH results from conditions that have an extra-abdominal origin (e.g., sepsis, major burns or other conditions requiring massive fluid resuscitation) [3].

atoms.statement: Tertiary IAH refers to the more chronic condition of an open and frozen abdomen after initial treatment for either primary or secondary IAH.

evidence.section: Intra-abdominal Hypertension and Abdominal Compartment Syndrome
evidence.text: Tertiary IAH refers to the more chronic condition of an open and frozen abdomen after initial treatment for either primary or secondary IAH.

atoms.statement: The IAP measurement standard is intermittent estimation via the bladder, with a maximal instillation of 20 to 25 mL of sterile saline through a urinary catheter, at end-expiration in the supine position with no abdominal muscle contractions, with the transducer zeroed where the midaxillary line crosses the iliac crest.

evidence.section: Intra-abdominal Hypertension and Abdominal Compartment Syndrome
evidence.text: However, the gold standard for intermittent IAP estimation is via the bladder with a maximal instillation of 20–25 mL (1 mL/kg in children up to 10 kg) of sterile saline through a urinary catheter.

evidence.section: Intra-abdominal Hypertension and Abdominal Compartment Syndrome
evidence.text: The transducer should be zeroed at the level where the midaxillary line crosses the iliac crest and IAP should be expressed in mmHg (conversion factor from mmHg to cmH2O is 1.36).

evidence.text: IAP should be measured at end-expiration in the supine position whilst abdominal muscle contractions are absent.

atoms.statement: Volume kinetics is an elaboration of the hemodilution concept that captures flows of fluid between body fluid compartments over time, and it has similarities to pharmacokinetics.

evidence.text: The hemodilution concept can be elaborated upon to capture flows of fluid between body fluid compartments over time.
This approach is called volume kinetics and has similarities to pharmacokinetics.

atoms.statement: Volume kinetics differs from conventional pharmacokinetics in that the walls of the body fluid compartments are expandable, and in that its input variable is hemodilution rather than plasma drug concentration.

evidence.text: One important difference is that the walls of the body fluid compartments are expandable [21].
Another difference is the choice of input variable.
conventional pharmacokinetics, the plasma concentration of the drug to be studied serves as the input.
For volume kinetics, hemodilution is used to capture the distribution of the infused water volume.

atoms.statement: Volume kinetics is an adaptation of pharmacokinetic theory that makes it possible to analyze and simulate the distribution and elimination of infusion fluids.

evidence.text: Volume kinetics is an adaptation of pharmacokinetic theory that makes it possible to
analyze and simulate the distribution and elimination of infusion fluids [35].

atoms.statement: Volume kinetics is based on serial analysis of blood hemoglobin concentration and, at best, urine volume during and after infusion of a fluid in a controlled setting, and blood volume itself is not important to the calculations.

evidence.text: The blood volume is not important to the calculations, but volume kinetics is still based
on serial analysis of the blood Hb concentration and, at best, the urine volume as well, during and after infusion of a fluid in a controlled setting.

atoms.statement: The rise in blood water concentration after a fluid infusion only seems analogous to a drug concentration in pharmacokinetics, because it represents a dilution of the administered water in a much larger water volume, which adds requirements to the calculations.

evidence.text: The increase in the blood water concentration then seems to yield the same concept as a drug concentration in conventional pharmacokinetics.
Sadly, though, this is an illusion, because the rise in blood water concentration that occurs when a fluid is infused represents a dilution of administered water in a much larger water volume.
This fact adds some requirements to the calculations.

atoms.statement: In volume kinetics, hemodilution (decreased blood Hb, hence increased blood water) is used to capture the distribution of the infused water volume, but the rise in blood water concentration is only an apparent analogue of a drug concentration because it represents infused water diluted in a much larger water volume, which adds requirements to the calculations.

evidence.text: For volume kinetics, hemodilution is used to capture the distribution of the infused water volume.
With regard to volume, the blood contains almost exclusively Hb and water.
If Hb is decreased, the water component of the blood is increased.

atoms.statement: By simulation using volume kinetics, one can determine the infusion rate required to reach a predetermined plasma volume expansion.

evidence.text: Applying this concept, it is possible, by simulation, to determine the infusion rate that is required to reach a predetermined plasma volume expansion.

atoms.statement: Volume kinetic analysis has shown that after expansion by a crystalloid fluid the interstitial fluid space is only twice as large as the plasma volume, which is less than commonly assumed, and crystalloid distribution has a half-life of 8 min.

evidence.text: The results have shown that the interstitial fluid space after expansion by a crystalloid fluid is only twice as large as the plasma volume, i.e., less than commonly assumed.
The distribution of crystalloid fluid occurs with a half-life of 8 min, except in association with an abrupt drop in arterial pressure, when distribution is temporarily arrested.

atoms.statement: During general anesthesia, elimination of crystalloid fluid is greatly retarded owing to reduced arterial pressure, whereas the intravascular persistence of colloid fluid does not seem to be affected by arterial pressure.

evidence.text: The elimination of crystalloid fluid is greatly retarded during general anesthesia due to
the reduction in arterial pressure [21].
By contrast, the intravascular persistence of a colloid fluid does not seem to be affected by the arterial pressure.

atoms.statement: Volume kinetic results show crystalloid distribution occurs with a half-life of 8 min except in association with an abrupt drop in arterial pressure, when distribution is temporarily arrested, so that during such a drop it does not matter whether a crystalloid or a colloid is infused.

evidence.text: The distribution of crystalloid fluid occurs with a half-life of 8 min, except in association with an abrupt drop in arterial pressure, when distribution is temporarily arrested.
Hence, when the blood pressure drops, it does not matter if one infuses a crystalloid or a colloid fluid.

atoms.statement: The volume kinetic calculations of colloid-versus-crystalloid effectiveness do not assume any injury to the endothelial glycocalyx layer.

evidence.text: These calculations do not assume any injury to the endothelial glycocalyx layer.

atoms.statement: Recent human investigations are reported to confirm animal laboratory evidence that some sodium is stored within the body without commensurate water, contrary to the teaching that body sodium content directly determines extracellular fluid volume.

evidence.section: Lymphatics and the Interstitial Storage of Sodium
evidence.text: It has long been taught that body sodium content directly determines the extracellular fluid volume and therefore the effective circulating fluid volume.

evidence.section: Lymphatics and the Interstitial Storage of Sodium
evidence.text: Recent investigations in humans confirm animal laboratory evidence that some sodium is in fact stored within the body without commensurate water.

atoms.statement: The body's sodium store is described as an interstitial reservoir that buffers free extracellular sodium and is regulated by extrarenal, tissue-specific mechanisms for sodium release and storage.

evidence.section: Lymphatics and the Interstitial Storage of Sodium
evidence.text: The sodium store is now shown to be an interstitial reservoir that buffers the free extracellular sodium and is regulated by extrarenal, tissue-specific mechanisms for the release and storage of sodium.

atoms.statement: The major anatomic site of extrarenal sodium regulation is the skin interstitium, which has a substantial volume of interstitial fluid and a lymphatic vessel network that can be expanded or reduced according to long-term sodium intake.

evidence.section: Lymphatics and the Interstitial Storage of Sodium
evidence.text: The major anatomic site of this sodium regulation is the interstitium of the skin, with its substantial volume of interstitial fluid and lymphatic vasculature forming a vessel network that can be expanded or reduced according to long-term sodium intake.

atoms.statement: PI3K phosphorylates Akt (also known as protein kinase B), a serine/threonine kinase, and activation of the PI3K-Akt cascade stimulates Bcl-2 family members that act as anti-apoptotic factors.

evidence.section: 1.4 Intracellular Signal Transduction Triggered by Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptors
evidence.text: PI3K phosphorylates Akt (or known as protein kinase B), a serine/threonine kinase.

evidence.text: Activation of PI3-Akt cascade stimulates B-cell lymphoma 2 (Bcl-2) family members, which act as anti-apoptotic factors.

atoms.statement: In the authors' proposed model of nAChR-mediated survival signaling, stimulation of α7 nAChRs activates the Src family, which activates PI3K, which phosphorylates Akt and thereby upregulates the anti-apoptotic proteins Bcl-2 and Bcl-x.

evidence.section: 8.4 Neuroprotective Enhancement of nAChRs Through Four Pathways (Kawamata and Shimohama 2011)
evidence.text: From the experimental data, our hypothesis for the mechanism of nAChR-mediated survival signal transduction
is as follows: activation of α7 nAChRs stimulates the Src family, which in turn activates PI3K.
PI3K phosphorylates AKT, which causes upregulation of Bcl-2 and Bcl-x. α4β2 nAChR stimulation also causes neuroprotection cascade without direct involvement of PI3K system.

atoms.statement: Neuroprotection from persistent nAChR stimulation is described not by simple excitatory depolarization from ion channel opening but by activation of the intracellular PI3K-Akt pathway leading to upregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2, with the highly Ca2+-permeable α7 nAChR playing a crucial role.

evidence.text: Mechanisms of neuroprotective effects exerted by persistent nAChR stimulation cannot be described only by simple excitatory reactions following depolarization induced by ion channel openings, but rather by activation of the intracellular PI3K-Akt signaling pathway leading to up-regulation of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2. α7 nAChR, which shows high Ca2+ permeability, plays a crucial role in nicotinic neuroprotection.

atoms.statement: In cultured cortical neurons, 24 h nicotine treatment increased Bcl-2 and Bcl-x protein levels, and LY294002 inhibited this increase, indicating involvement of the PI3K pathway in nicotine-induced Bcl-2 and Bcl-x upregulation.

evidence.section: 8.2.2 Nicotine Protects Neurons Against Aβ Toxicity In Vitro
evidence.text: We found that treatment with nicotine for 24 h increased the levels of Bcl-2 and Bcl-x, and this was inhibited by LY294002, which indicates the involvement of the PI3K pathway in nicotine-induced Bcl-2 and Bcl-x upregulation.

atoms.statement: In cultured cortical neurons, nicotine-induced Akt phosphorylation was blocked by the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 but not by the MEK inhibitor PD98059, indicating that PI3K rather than MAPK is involved.

evidence.section: 8.2.2 Nicotine Protects Neurons Against Aβ Toxicity In Vitro
evidence.text: The phosphorylated form of AKT appeared immediately after the application of nicotine.

evidence.text: Nicotine-induced AKT phosphorylation was blocked by simultaneous application of LY294002, but not of PD98059, indicating that PI3K, but not MAPK is involved.

atoms.statement: Studies testing nicotine and other nAChR agonists in experimental models of ischemic injury gave conflicting results: some reported beneficial effects and others reported deleterious effects.

evidence.text: In contrast, studies addressing the effects of nAChR agonists on experimental ischemic injury models gave conflicting results, where some studies reported beneficial effects but others demonstrated deleterious effects.

atoms.statement: Studies reporting beneficial effects of nicotine and nAChR agonists in experimental ischemia generally used daily administration only a few times, or low doses when treatment was long-term.

evidence.text: On the other hand, studies reporting beneficial effects of nicotine and nAChR agonists generally performed daily administration of the drugs for a few times or low-dose administration in the case of long-term treatment.

atoms.statement: Virtually all experimental ischemia studies reporting deleterious effects of nicotine used continuous delivery by osmotic pumps or repeated daily administration at relatively high doses.

evidence.text: Namely, virtually all studies reporting the deleterious effects of nicotine performed continuous delivery by osmotic pumps or repeated daily administration of nicotine at relatively high doses.

evidence.text: An early study by Wang et al. (1997) examined the effect of nicotine (4.5 mg/kg/day) administered subcutaneously for 14 days by osmotic minipumps, prior to induction of ischemic insults in rats.

Interestingly, nicotine-treated rats exhibited depletion of tissue plasminogen activator in cerebral capillaries, which might be causally relevant to the poor recovery of the blood flow after reperfusion and to the resultant exacerbation of brain tissue injury.

evidence.text: Based on the findings in slice culture preparations, we initially examined the effect of long-term pretreatment of nicotine (1 mg/kg, intraperitoneally once per day for 1 week) and obtained cytoprotective effect of nicotine on striatal neurons within the hematoma assessed at 3 days after induction of ICH (our unpublished observations).

evidence.section: 7.4.1 Effects of nAChR Agonists on Intracerebral Hemorrhage (ICH)
evidence.text: However, the long-term pretreatment regimen is unrealistic for ICH pharmacotherapy in clinical practice, so we next examined the effect of nicotine in a post-­treatment regimen.

atoms.statement: The authors reason that, because Aβ concentrations in the CSF of AD patients are almost 100 times higher than in plasma, creating a large brain-to-plasma gradient, removing Aβ from the blood could accelerate Aβ transfer from the brain and thereby reduce brain Aβ burden.
